cells.tense: You are meeting what is coming in and telling it plainly where to go.
cells.act: cut to the logic and act on it
cells.ask: Work out what the new thing actually is and what it's for — two clean sentences, no hedging — then take one concrete step. Ten minutes is enough.
cells.core:
Something has your attention that wasn't there before — a person, a chance, an idea still half-lit — and you can meet it without deciding it in advance. You say what it is, you put words to what pulls at you, and you don't lose your footing doing it. That's the shape: the enthusiasm shows early and you let people see it, then you don't walk it back later.

Your mind already does the cutting well. Turn it on the new thing. Work out what it actually is and what it's for, two clean sentences, no hedging — then take the next concrete step. Ten minutes is enough. Nothing you work out here is a promise; the test is only whether acting gets easier afterward.
cells.sheetLine: You can name what's arriving and still move.
cells.verb: striking a new fire and pointing where it goes
cells.place: the doorway where what is arriving first reaches you

cells.tense: You are bracing for how this will go wrong before it has even arrived.
cells.act: perceive it with fresh eyes before judging
cells.ask: Before settling anything about the new thing, write three observations you wouldn't have made yesterday. Three lines, no verdict, no plan.
cells.core:
The way you meet something new is by working out its future first. You run the next three moves, the risk, the likely failure, and you're usually right — but the running is what you're doing now, not the meeting. The fire gets checked before it burns, and what's arriving is the checking, not whatever came through the door.

Try the other end, once. Take the new thing as it actually is, before anything about it is settled, and write three observations you wouldn't have made yesterday. Three lines, no verdict, no plan. Unfamiliarity doesn't need managing yet — that's what you find out.

cells.tense: You are still standing in a doorway something already walked through.
cells.act: care for it with fresh hands and see what it needs
cells.ask: Choose anything near you that's already yours to keep — a plant, a shelf, a page — give it ten minutes, and see what it asks of you.
cells.core:
Something is arriving and you're not at the door. The urge to start is there, but your hand doesn't reach; you wait for the feeling to be finished before you'd let anyone see it, and by then whatever was coming has moved on. It reads as patience. It's more like standing slightly behind where your own life is.

Come at it through your hands instead. Choose anything near you that's already yours to keep — a plant, a shelf, a page — and spend ten minutes with it. See what it asks of you. That's the same move a spark needs, at a size you can hold this week. The fire comes back once the hands have somewhere to go.

cells.tense: You are opening doors and calling it the weather.
cells.act: hold the weight as a builder holds stone
cells.ask: Take something that only works if you keep showing up for it, and show up this week — same time, no announcement.
cells.core:
You can walk into a new room and get the whole thing moving — you start things, people follow, and you'd describe your part as going along with it. The starting is happening, and it's yours, and the language you use about it leaves you out. The people who followed you don't leave you out.

Come back to the plain version. Take something that only works if you keep showing up for it, and show up this week — same time, no announcement. That's the same act as the big one, at a size that lets you feel the author's hand on it, from the inside.

The asks survive being wrong because each one is small and gives something back whether or not my read is right — you learn what's entering either way. The sentence I'd be serving is the pretty 'spark before it knows where it's going' one; it makes a nice line and tells the person nothing. So it stays in my head, not the cell.
